Name: hallucination_weak_enrichment
Title: Filling the Void: Weak Subject Enrichment as a Signature of Hallucination
Short Hypothesis: Factual hallucinations occur disproportionately when subject enrichment is weak-i.e., the recall locus carries little attribute information-because the model, lacking a stored answer, falls back on fluent plausible completion; the magnitude of enrichment (locus state norm/probe strength) is a training-free predictor of hallucination that outperforms output entropy. Hallucination is the absence of retrieval, not corrupted retrieval.
Related Work: Hallucination detection uses output uncertainty (semantic entropy; Kuhn et al., 2023) and self-consistency. Mechanistic signals are emerging (e.g., internal 'truthfulness' probes). We propose a specific, mechanistically-motivated signal-enrichment weakness at the subject recall locus-and test that it beats uncertainty baselines and localizes WHY the model hallucinates (nothing to retrieve), not just that it does.
Abstract: When a model states a confident falsehood about an entity, is it retrieving a wrong fact or retrieving nothing and confabulating? We hypothesize the latter dominates: hallucinations coincide with weak subject enrichment at the recall locus, where little attribute information is present, prompting fluent guesswork. We measure enrichment strength via the norm of the attribute-carrying component and the peak of an attribute probe at the subject position, and test that (i) hallucinated answers show significantly weaker enrichment than correct ones; (ii) enrichment strength predicts hallucination better than output-side uncertainty measures; and (iii) for entities the model was never exposed to, enrichment is near baseline, confirming the 'nothing to retrieve' account. We evaluate on factual QA with known-vs-unknown entities across models, comparing enrichment-based detection to semantic entropy and self-consistency, and analyzing false positives. Establishing weak enrichment as a hallucination signature would give a cheap, single-forward-pass detector, mechanistically explain confabulation as retrieval absence, and distinguish it from a separate failure mode where strong-but-wrong retrieval occurs-guiding different mitigations for each.
Experiments: 1. Build QA with correct, incorrect (hallucinated), and unknown-entity items. 2. Compute enrichment strength (attribute-component norm, probe peak) at the subject locus. 3. Compare enrichment across outcome classes. 4. Benchmark enrichment-based hallucination detection (AUC) vs semantic entropy and self-consistency. 5. Analyze unknown entities for baseline-level enrichment. Metrics: enrichment by class, detection AUC vs baselines, unknown-entity enrichment, false-positive analysis (strong-but-wrong cases).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Defining the enrichment component precisely is method-dependent. Some hallucinations may involve strong-but-wrong retrieval, capping detector recall. Correlation with frequency may drive results. Generalization from short QA to long-form generation is uncertain.
